nameStory: The word 'moose' comes from the Algonquian word 'moos' or 'moz,' meaning 'twig eater' – a perfect name for an animal that munches on woody branches all winter long. Early European settlers adopted this Native American term, which has stuck for over 400 years. Interestingly, what we call a moose in North America is called an elk in Europe, which can confuse visitors from across the pond!
description: The moose is New England's gentle giant – the world's largest deer and our region's most massive wild animal. Picture a horse-sized creature with long, skinny legs, a humped shoulder, and a droopy nose, and you're getting close. Adult moose can stand 6 feet tall at the shoulder and weigh as much as a small car. Male moose sport massive, flat antlers that can span 6 feet across, looking like giant open hands reaching toward the sky.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Enormous size with impossibly long legs that make them look like they're walking on stilts. The distinctive humped shoulders and pendulous nose (called a bell) create an unmistakable silhouette that towers over any other New England mammal.

idTips.label: Antlers
idTips.description: Males grow massive, flat, palm-shaped antlers that feel rough like sandpaper and can be wider than a person is tall. These 'paddles' are completely different from the pointed, branching antlers of other deer – think open hands rather than tree branches.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dark brown to nearly black coat that feels coarse and hollow when touched, with longer guard hairs that help shed water. The fur often appears shaggy and unkempt, especially around the neck and shoulders where it forms a distinctive mane.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Massive heart-shaped hoofprints, each track as big as your outstretched hand or larger. In soft mud, you can see how the two halves of each hoof spread apart under the animal's enormous weight, leaving deep, clear impressions.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Solitary and surprisingly quiet for such large animals – you'll often hear splashing before seeing one feeding in wetlands. They move with a distinctive high-stepping gait and will often freeze statue-still when they notice you watching.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Browse lines on young trees and shrubs at 6-8 feet high (much higher than deer), plus large, oval droppings that look like oversized rabbit pellets scattered in piles. Broken branches and stripped bark on saplings show where they've been feeding.

habitat: Moose love New England's wet places – you'll find them wading in marshes, bogs, shallow ponds, and beaver meadows where they feed on aquatic plants. They also frequent mixed and coniferous forests with dense understory growth, especially areas with young aspen, birch, and willow. Look for them anywhere water meets woods, from mountain ponds to lowland swamps.

seasonality.spring: Moose shed their thick winter coats in patchy clumps, often looking quite raggedy. Females with new calves become extremely protective and potentially dangerous if approached.
seasonality.summer: Most active during cool dawn and dusk hours, often standing belly-deep in water to feed on aquatic plants and escape biting insects. Their sleek summer coat shows off their true size and muscle definition.
seasonality.fall: Bulls grow aggressive during mating season (September-October) and sport their largest, most impressive antlers. Listen for their haunting calls echoing across wetlands at dawn and dusk.
seasonality.winter: Males drop their antlers, leaving just small bumps on their heads. Their thick, dark winter coat makes them look even more massive as they browse on woody twigs and bark.

funFact: Moose are surprisingly excellent swimmers and can dive up to 20 feet deep to munch on underwater plants – they're the only deer that can hold their breath and feed completely submerged, essentially becoming temporary aquatic mammals!
confusionNotes: At a distance, moose might be confused with horses or large cattle, but no domestic animal has that distinctive droopy nose, humped shoulders, and impossibly long legs. Remember: if it looks like someone put a horse together wrong and made it too tall, it's probably a moose!
contextualKnowledge: What Americans call a moose, Europeans call an elk – and what Americans call an elk, Europeans call a red deer. This naming confusion dates back to early European settlers who mixed up the Native American and European names. If you're talking to someone from Europe about 'elk,' you might actually be discussing the same animal!
compareHints: Moose are the only species in their genus, making them unique among deer. Compared to their closest relatives like white-tailed deer or elk (wapiti), moose are much larger with distinctive flat antlers rather than pointed ones, longer legs, and that characteristic droopy nose. While other deer are built for speed and agility, moose are built like living bulldozers – massive, powerful, and unmistakable.
